events.note: Start indoors Jan-early Feb; pot on and grow cooler at 12-18 C (book p. 378).
Plant out once frost risk is over, after 20 May (book p. 378).
Cut heads as bracts open; finish by late September (book p. 379).

name: Sweetcorn
notes: Needs deep, rich soil in a sunny, sheltered spot; plant in square blocks, not rows, for pollination.
Keep supersweet varieties at least 100 m from ordinary corn. Water in drought and liquid-feed twice in summer.
Cover with fleece after planting out; pick when silks wither and kernels are creamy.
description: A tall grass that Columbus brought from the Americas to Europe, where it spread worldwide within decades. In Sweden it's grown for its sweet cobs, and also for popcorn.
howToEat: Cobs are best boiled fresh. Blanch them before freezing. Popcorn varieties can be grown for popping.

events.note: Sow 2 seeds per 10 cm pot 3-4 weeks before planting out (book p. 379).
Plant out after frost risk once soil is at least 12 C; cover with fleece (book p. 380).
Pick when silks have withered and kernels are creamy; finish by late September (book p. 380).

name: Asparagus
notes: Needs sun and light, deep soil cleared of perennial weeds; double-dig and add plenty of compost.
Plant crowns in 30 cm trenches with a central ridge, filling in through summer; feed yearly after harvest.
Cut down in autumn. Earth up or add sand in spring for white spears.
description: A long-lived perennial that sends up finger-thick, juicy shoots each spring, then grows into a feathery hedge. It has been grown for over 5,000 years, including by the Egyptians, and comes as white (blanched) or green.
howToEat: Eat the young spring shoots. Green asparagus tastes just as good as white, and some varieties, like Primaverde, are good raw in salads.

events.note: Soak seed 1-2 days and sow in pots indoors at about 20 C (book p. 382).
Plant the seedlings into the prepared trench once frost is over (after 20 May).
Seed-grown plants need longer to establish than bought crowns before the first cutting. Then cut spears at 18–20 cm until midsummer. Most people buy crowns (book p. 382).
Plant crowns in trenches when the soil is workable (book p. 383).
Cut spears at 18-20 cm until midsummer; start 3 years after planting crowns (book p. 383).

name: Cardoon
notes: Grow like artichoke; perennial but treated as annual, 1-2 m tall with silvery leaves.
Blanch stems for a month before harvest by wrapping in corrugated card; strip coarse strings before cooking.
description: The ancestor of the artichoke: a striking plant one to two metres tall with silvery leaves, grown for its stalks. It was common in grand 1800s kitchen gardens.
howToEat: Strip the tough strings from the blanched stalks, as with rhubarb. Italians boil them and eat them with olive oil and herb butter.

events.note: Start indoors as for artichoke (book p. 386).
Plant out once frost risk is over, after 20 May (book p. 386).
Blanch from late August and harvest in September before frost risk.

name: Angelica
notes: Wants rich, loose, moist soil in a not too warm spot.
Flowers in year two then dies; collect seed and resow, and it often self-seeds.
Peel stems like rhubarb; blanching makes them more tender.
description: A tall plant that grows wild in the Swedish mountains, where the Sami once harvested its young leaves and shoots. Its stalks taste slightly sweet.
howToEat: Peel the stalks, like rhubarb, and eat them; candied stalks are a delicious treat. Young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or boiled, the leaves make tea, and boiled flowers were eaten like cauliflower.

events.note: Sow fresh seed direct in autumn (book p. 387).
Cut young stems before flowering (book p. 387).

name: Sea kale
notes: Protected in the wild, so never dig plants; buy seed such as Lily White.
Plant in deep, loose, well-fed soil. Force in spring under an upturned bucket for 5-6 weeks.
Usually overwinters in central Sweden but not always; keep seed in reserve.
description: A perennial coastal plant that grows wild in southern Sweden, where it is protected in many places. Its blanched leaf stalks turn pale yellow and tender.
howToEat: The blanched leaf stalks are eaten as an early spring treat, in the same class as asparagus.

events.note: Sow fresh seed in pots in autumn and leave outside under fleece for the cold (book p. 387).
Plant out in deep, loose, well-fed soil (book p. 387).
Cut blanched shoots at 15 cm, from two years after sowing (book p. 387).

name: Aubergine
notes: Grow like tomato but warmer; ideal day temperature 22 C or more, so best in a pot in the greenhouse.
Liquid-feed every other week once flowering and pot on into a bucket-sized container.
Hose daily against whitefly and aphids; pick before the skin loses its gloss.
description: A heat-loving plant from India with woolly grey-green leaves and lavender-blue flowers. Fruits can be small and green, or white and egg-shaped (hence 'eggplant'), but modern varieties are mostly large and dark purple.
howToEat: Only the fruit is eaten; the leaves are poisonous.

events.note: Sow indoors in February or early March; give a sunny window and grow light (book p. 388).
Move out when nights stay at 12 C or more, in a pot in the greenhouse (book p. 388).
Pick at full size while the skin is still glossy (book p. 390).

name: Ground cherry
notes: Grow like tomato in a sunny, warm spot, in the ground or a bucket; 60-100 cm tall.
Hardier than tomato. Fruit is ripe when the husk yellows and berries drop.
description: A bushy North American plant, 60–100 cm tall, with golden berries wrapped in a papery lantern. The berries are sweet with a wild aroma.
howToEat: Best eaten fresh, and used in cakes, pies and other desserts. Eat only fully ripe berries with the papery husk removed; unripe berries are poisonous.

events.note: Sow indoors as for tomato, 8-10 weeks before planting out (book p. 394, 400).
Plant out after 20 May in a warm, sunny spot or a bucket (book p. 400).
Pick when husks turn yellow and fruit falls; finish by late September (book p. 400).

name: Tomatillo
notes: Grow like a bush tomato in the greenhouse or a sheltered spot, ideally in a large, well-fed bucket.
Prune if too bushy. Pick fruit green and unripe, mainly for salsa verde.
description: A relative of the ground cherry, taller and with fruits almost twice the size, each inside a papery husk. The flavour is a bit like tomato, but very much its own.
howToEat: Pick the fruits green and blend with coriander, onion, chilli and garlic for salsa verde. Also good in meat sauce, but not raw in salads.

events.note: Sow indoors as for tomato, 8-10 weeks before planting out (book p. 394, 400).
Plant in a large bucket in the greenhouse (book p. 400).
Pick green; fairly frost-tolerant and crops into autumn (book p. 401).

name: Arctic bramble
notes: Plant two or more varieties for pollination, in moist, loose soil rich in compost; pH matters little.
Water well during flowering and fruit set, feed lightly after year two, and renew the patch from runners every 5-8 years.
Shares pests such as the raspberry beetle with raspberry and blackberry, so keep it away from them; too much nitrogen invites grey mould.
description: A cross between wild arctic bramble and its Alaskan relative that spreads into a pretty ground cover with pink flowers. The dark red berries taste almost as heavenly as wild ones; yields are highest in the north.
howToEat: Pick when dark red and slightly soft; makes an exquisite liqueur and jam (book p. 470).

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (book p. 470).
Or plant in early autumn (book p. 470); new runners can also be moved in autumn.
Flowers early June, berries a month later (book p. 470); expect 1-3 weeks later in Stockholm. Full crop from year three.

name: Blackberry
notes: Needs a warm spot, ideally against a south wall, in deep, light, well-drained soil; tie canes to a wire trellis with wires 30 cm apart.
Keep first-year canes on the ground (cover them in winter with spruce branches or straw) and fan-train second-year canes; cut fruited canes out in autumn, leaving 6-8 new ones.
Grey mould is the main problem: thin the canes and avoid excess nitrogen. Raspberry beetle larvae can also attack.
description: A rambling cane fruit that grows wild as far north as the Stockholm region; gardens now mainly grow thornless varieties. Canes fruit in their second year and the harvest runs through autumn.

events.note: Plant in spring in a warm, sheltered spot; cut bare-root plants back to 30 cm (book p. 471).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Harvest continues all autumn, but in cool summers not all berries ripen (book p. 471); frost risk from late September in Stockholm.

name: Blueberry
notes: Needs acid soil (pH 4-5.5): fill a 30 cm deep, 60 cm wide hole (deeper and wider in clay) with unfertilised peat mixed with composted bark, or rhododendron soil, and mulch with conifer litter.
Plant two varieties for better pollination, prune to 30 cm at planting, and after three years cut out about a fifth of the oldest and drooping branches each year.
Keep the soil constantly moist and protect flowers from frost with fleece; net against birds, hares and deer.
description: Garden blueberries taste milder and sweeter than wild ones, are two to three times larger and have white flesh that won't stain your mouth. Highbush is the commonest type, giving 2-7 kg per bush, with orange-red autumn colour.
howToEat: The berries are firm and can be eaten fresh or frozen individually (book p. 472).

events.note: Plant in spring, no deeper than in the pot, in a sunny, acid bed (book p. 474).
Or plant in autumn (book p. 474), early enough to root before the freeze.
The book gives no month; midsummer to late summer is an estimate for Stockholm.

name: Blueberry
notes: Needs acid soil (pH 4-5.5): plant in a hole filled with unfertilised peat and composted bark, or rhododendron soil, raised slightly above ground; mulch with conifer litter.
Plant at least two varieties for pollination, prune to 30 cm at planting, and after three years remove about a fifth of the oldest branches yearly.
Keep moist, cover flowers if frost threatens, and net against birds, hares and deer.
description: A cross between highbush and wild blueberry: lower (60-100 cm), slightly less productive and wilder in flavour, but more cold-hardy than highbush. A Swedish fruit research station bred the hardy variety Putte.
howToEat: The berries are firm and can be eaten fresh or frozen individually (book p. 472).

events.note: Plant in spring, no deeper than in the pot, in a sunny, acid bed (book p. 474).
Or plant in autumn (book p. 474), early enough to root before the freeze.
The book gives no month; midsummer to late summer is an estimate for Stockholm.

name: Haskap
notes: Not self-pollinating: plant two or three varieties in sun and moist soil rich in organic matter; avoids heavy clay.
Feed moderately with manure in spring; no pruning for the first 5-6 years, then thin like a currant bush.
Very healthy, but can get fungal disease in too much shade. Flowers early but tolerate about -7 to -8 °C.
description: A blue honeysuckle transformed by 60 years of Canadian and Russian breeding into a large, sweet-tart, very vitamin-rich berry. Extremely hardy, and it ripens about a week before strawberries.
howToEat: The berries are used just like blueberries and other garden berries (book p. 476).

events.note: Plant once the soil is workable; berry bushes can go in as soon as you can dig (book p. 466).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Ripens about a week before strawberries (book p. 476); late June to early July in Stockholm.

name: Saskatoon
notes: Self-fertile but needs insects to pollinate; grows in most well-drained, porous soils in sun or light shade.
Top new plants to 25-30 cm for more branches; start pruning after 6-7 years, removing 20% of the oldest and drooping branches yearly.
Water in drought or the berries drop; birds are the only real pest.
description: A North American relative of the serviceberry, used for centuries as food and medicine from Maine to Alaska. Clouds of white blossom, orange-red autumn leaves, and berries tasting of wild blueberry with a hint of blackcurrant.
howToEat: Eat the berries when they turn from pink to dark purple; they taste like wild blueberries with a touch of blackcurrant and were long used as food by Native Americans (book p. 478).

events.note: Plant once the soil is workable; berry bushes can go in as soon as you can dig (book p. 466).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Ripens early to mid July (book p. 478), likely mid to late July in Stockholm; pick when berries turn dark purple.

name: Sea buckthorn
notes: Female plants need a male nearby for wind pollination: one male per five females. Plant in full sun; light soil is best, lighten heavy clay.
Nitrogen-fixing and drought-tolerant, so feed sparingly but water for bigger crops. Roots spread aggressively, so plant in a corner and chop runners.
Prune to 40-50 cm at planting; protect young shoots from hares and deer with netting.
description: A tough shrub with silvery leaves and very sour orange berries tasting of passion fruit and pineapple. The berries hold three times as much vitamin C as oranges.
howToEat: Too sour to eat raw without sugar; use for parfait, sorbet, panna cotta, marmalade, cordial or a fresh-pressed health shot. Easiest harvest: cut whole branches, freeze them and shake the berries off (book p. 484).

events.note: Spring planting is safest (book p. 484).
Potted plants can also go in in autumn (book p. 484).
The book gives no month; late summer to early autumn is an estimate for Stockholm. Cut whole branches and freeze.

name: Gooseberry
notes: Very sparing with nitrogen, which strongly encourages powdery mildew; feed with compost and potassium-rich wood ash instead.
From about year five, remove low-lying, damaged and the 3-4 oldest branches in late autumn or late winter.
Watch for gooseberry sawfly larvae, which can strip a bush quickly; pick them off by hand or use nematodes.
description: Gooseberry fever swept 1800s Sweden until powdery mildew wiped out the crops. Mildew-resistant varieties have brought a revival, and wild bushes from old homesteads can have unbeatable aroma.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, 5 cm deeper than before; cut bare-root plants back to 30 cm (book p. 490).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Lingonberry
notes: Acid-soil plant planted like blueberry; needs almost no fertiliser and too much will harm it.
Don't let it dry out, especially in June and July.
Rejuvenate after 10-15 years by cutting down to a few centimetres above the ground.
description: Cultivated lingonberries are compact evergreen plants with big red berries that taste like wild ones, making a fine edging. Each plant gives 0.5-1 litre a year from year three.

events.note: The book says plant in spring, in acid soil as for blueberries (book p. 492).
Berries ripen mid-August in the book (p. 491); allow a week or two later in Stockholm. Variety Ida repeat-flowers for a second crop.

name: Wild strawberry
notes: Sunny spot in decent garden soil, cleared of perennial weeds and enriched with manure and compost.
Drought tolerant, but watering during fruiting raises yield; renew plants after 3-4 years from runners or by dividing alpine types.
Strawberry leaf beetle can riddle the leaves in hot, dry summers; try spraying soapy water before flowering.
description: Non-running alpine strawberries make superb edging and fruit all summer; newer runner-forming red and white types have bigger berries and are effective ground cover.

events.note: Plant in spring or early autumn (book p. 492).
Set out runners straight after harvest, or divide alpine plants, in late summer to early autumn.
Alpine types such as Rügen fruit all summer; runner types crop over a shorter period.

name: Tayberry
notes: Needs a warm, sunny spot, ideally trained on a south-facing wall like blackberry; cut bare-root plants back by two thirds.
Fruits on two-year canes: cut fruited canes out in autumn after harvest and lay young canes on the ground under spruce branches or straw for winter.
Gets the same pests and diseases as blackberry and raspberry.
description: A 1970s Scottish raspberry-blackberry hybrid, the best of the 'bramble-raspberries'. Deep red berries 4 cm long, on long thorny canes; keep flavour expectations modest.
howToEat: Picked when dark red and eaten fresh; the book says the berries look like jewels on a cream cake.

events.note: Plant against a sunny south wall with support in spring.
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes.
Ripens a few days before raspberry, usually late July in the book (p. 494); expect late July-August in Stockholm.

name: Currant
notes: Wants full sun and moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; feed sparingly.

Flowers on two-year-old and older wood, so start thinning after 4-5 years and prune more lightly than black currant. Prune at the base in autumn or winter: remove drooping and damaged branches and the 3-4 oldest each year.
Aphids cause reddish blisters on the leaves, mainly on red currants; spray with water or soapy water.
description: Very hardy currant grown throughout Sweden. An old Dutch red variety, around 300 years old, gives small berries but a high yield and is hardy to zone 6.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, as for gooseberry (book p. 497).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical mid-late summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Currant
notes: Wants full sun and moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; feed sparingly.
Pruned like red currant: flowers on two-year-old wood, start thinning after 4-5 years. Prune at the base in autumn or winter: remove drooping and damaged branches and the 3-4 oldest each year.
Pink currants such as Pink Champagne (a red x white cross) are grown the same way but only to zone 2.
description: White currants arose as a mutation of red currants and are slightly milder in taste, as are pink currants.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, as for gooseberry (book p. 497).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical mid-late summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Elder
notes: Likes humus-rich, fertile soil; feed every spring.
Aphids love it; after a few years thin out old, woody branches.
Stands still for a few years after planting, then grows fast; good as a screen or hedge.
description: A large shrub that grows up to four metres high and wide once established. Varieties Samyl and Samidan stay at two to three metres.
howToEat: Both the flowers and the berries are used for cordial. Do not confuse it with red-berried elder (Sambucus racemosa), whose red berries are not edible (book p. 503). Always cook the berries: raw or unripe elderberries, leaves and stems can make you sick.

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (late April-May in Stockholm).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. A sucker from a wild elder also works.
Flowers for cordial; timing not given in the book, typically around midsummer in Stockholm.
Berries for cordial; timing not given in the book.

name: Magnolia vine
notes: Usually has separate male and female plants, so buy a self-fertile (monoecious) plant if you only grow one.
Plant in porous, fertile soil in a sheltered spot, ideally against a south wall; let two shoots climb a support and feed moderately.
Propagate from side shoots; the book says sowing seed also works well.
description: Also called schisandra, the most challenging berry in the chapter: a climbing vine with lemon-scented flowers and leaves and clusters of lingonberry-red berries.
howToEat: The berries are used for cordial and a jelly said to go well with game; Siberian hunters used them against hunger and fatigue.

events.note: Plant in a sheltered, warm spot once the soil is workable; the book gives zones 1-2 (3), so it may struggle in Stockholm.
Berry clusters glow red in July-August in the book (p. 502); expect a week or two later in Stockholm.

name: Cloudberry
notes: Needs male and female plants (at least one male per nine females); only variety Nyby is self-fertile.
Recreate a bog: constantly moist, low-pH light peat mixed with reindeer lichen, ideally in a watertight basin and partial shade.
Needs almost no fertiliser; the flowers are frost-sensitive, so cover them on frosty nights.
description: A real challenge with low yields, but hardy to minus 40 degrees. New plants are easy from 10 cm rhizome pieces planted about 2 cm deep.

events.note: Plant into a prepared bog bed once the soil thaws, about 25 plants per square metre; protect flowers from late frosts (risk until about 20 May).
Rhizome pieces can be planted in early autumn so they root before the freeze.
Harvest timing not given in the book.

name: Rose hip
scientificName: Rosa dumalis, R. rugosa, R. rubiginosa
notes: All roses give hips, but dog rose, Japanese rose and sweet briar give the most and best.
Feed and water, keep weed-free for the first three years and scatter wood ash around the bush.
description: Grow your own hips instead of buying imported ones, and enjoy the roses too. Hips are packed with vitamin C, carotene and magnesium.
howToEat: Used for rose hip soup, a Swedish classic.

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (late April-May in Stockholm).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes.
Pick when bright red, ideally before the first frost nights (book p. 505); frost risk in Stockholm from about 25 September.

name: Black chokeberry
notes: Grown like black currant.
Robust and healthy; variety Hugin is hardy to zone 4.
description: The black berries taste of almost nothing but are rich in acid and dark pigment. Also an attractive ornamental with leaves that turn bright red in autumn.
howToEat: Useful for jelly and cordial thanks to their acidity and colour.

events.note: Plant as for black currant in spring.
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Harvest timing not given in the book.
